title: What's Different in the Blood of Centenarians
hook: Some people reach 100 in remarkably good health. A new study finds their blood carries a distinct chemical 'fingerprint' that sets them apart from typical aging.
key_points: Researchers compared the blood chemistry of centenarians to people aging typically.
Centenarians showed a distinct chemical 'fingerprint' rather than just a slower version of normal aging.
The differences centered on unusual patterns of bile acids and steroid compounds.
These specific patterns were linked to longer survival in the study.
content_html: Living past 100 in good health isn't just a matter of avoiding disease longer than everyone else — it may come with its own distinct biology. A new study finds that centenarians carry a chemical "fingerprint" in their blood that sets them apart from people experiencing typical aging.
extra_html: As ScienceDaily reports, the differences centered on unusual patterns of bile acids and steroid compounds, which the researchers linked to longer survival. The finding pushes against the simple idea that centenarians are just "aging normally, but slower" — instead, their biology looks qualitatively different in specific, measurable ways. That's useful for research, even if it's not yet actionable for anyone: identifying what a good "old age" looks like at the molecular level is a necessary first step before scientists can figure out whether any of it can be encouraged, rather than just observed.

related.title: The Thymus: A 'Forgotten' Organ Tied to Longevity
related.hook: The thymus was thought to clock out after childhood. A large imaging study found adults with healthier-looking thymuses tended to live longer — a striking link, not a prescription.

related.title: Aging Isn't Only Decline
related.hook: A long-term Yale study found nearly half of adults over 65 actually improved — physically, mentally, or both — and a more positive view of aging tracked with those gains.

related.title: The Supplements Older Adults Actually Need
related.hook: For most older adults, the real question isn't which trendy supplement to take — it's whether you have a specific deficiency. B12, vitamin D, and often-overlooked protein are where it matters.
